svg.title: Roll, Spin, Problem, Play - Computing Showcase poster (36 x 24 in)
svg.text: An adaptive VR math board game with a simulated AI Helper for second graders
Ahmet Nejdet Begdes · Efe Kaan Karaormanli
Department of Computer Science, UNC Wilmington
Original board game: Hannah Terry & Bailey Clark (EDN 303)

g.text: Board games link counting to space: a few short
sessions with a number board game improve young
VR keeps the feel of the real game – grab the die,
pull the handle, watch the piece hop – and adds
questions that adapt to each child.
Children also meet AI tools that can be wrong.
Robo teaches them to check, not just trust [2].
Grab the die with your LEFT hand, let go.
Your game piece hops by itself.
Hold the SPIN handle, press the trigger.
Point with your RIGHT hand and click.
Touch Robo. Is the AI Helper right?

svg.text: Seated · no walking · about 10 rolls per game
The classroom from the player's seat (illustration)

g.text: LEFT side: things you touch – Robo, die, handle, wheel
RIGHT side: the menu for the pointing ray
Starts at the classroom door, then a fade to your seat
2 right in a row → level up · 2 wrong → level down
Each third of the board unlocks a higher level,
so the hardest problems wait near FINISH.

svg.text: A wrong answer shows the right one with ten frames:

[1] R. S. Siegler and G. B. Ramani, "Playing linear numerical board games promotes low-income children's numerical development," Developmental Science, 2008. [2] D. Long and B. Magerko, "What is AI literacy? Competencies and design considerations," CHI 2020.
